## 🎯 The task

1. **Rebuild** your Lab 5 and Lab 7 models exactly as you submitted them, add MSTL, and run them on four
   rolling windows next to your benchmark. Everyone does this.
2. **Choose your track** — and write down what you expect *before* you run it:

   | Track | The idea | Lecture |
   |---|---|---|
   | **A. Combine** | an equal-weight average of your models | *Advanced Forecasting Methods* |
   | **B. Train** | MLP, N-BEATS, LSTM, trained on your series | *Neural Networks for Forecasting* |
   | **C. Borrow** | Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, zero-shot | *Foundation Models for Time Series* |
   | **D. Your own way** | all of the above, a mix of old and new, tuning, another model — anything you can defend | — |

3. **One scoreboard** for everything you ran, on the same four windows.
4. **Submit** what the scoreboard supports, with an 80% interval checked on windows it did not see.
5. **Conclude** against your Lab 5 and Lab 7 results — and say what you would use at work.

One track done well is a full-marks lab. More tracks, done with care, count toward the bonus.

**Not this time:** plots of the series, decomposition, ACF. Every plot is about the models.

## 🔁 Section 1 — Your models, rebuilt (1 point)

- `MEMBERS` holds your **submitted** Lab 5 ETS and Lab 7 seasonal ARIMA — the specification, the damping,
  the log — and MSTL, with a log decision of its own.
- `PAST` holds the hidden-horizon MASE and skill you were sent after Labs 5 and 7.
- The validation-window MASE **must match your earlier notebooks.** If it does not, find out why and say so.
- Two or three sentences: do the numbers match, and how do the three models stand on the four windows?
- Did not submit Lab 5 or Lab 7? Use the automatic model and say so; it costs nothing.

## 🎯 Section 2 — Forecast accuracy (3 points)

What you may submit: **any row of your scoreboard** — one forecaster, or an average you built with
`combine` — with an 80% interval, its own or conformal. Chosen on the rolling windows, never on anything
else. The template's `final_forecast` produces it from the whole history for you.

Scored from your submission file on the `h` observations after your history that nobody has seen:

$$
\text{skill} = \frac{\text{MASE of your forecast}}{\text{MASE of your benchmark}}
$$

| Skill | Points |
|---|---:|
| below 1 — you beat your benchmark | 3 |
| 1 to 1.1 — within 10% | 2 |
| above 1.1 | 1, and 3.3 must say why |

::: {.callout-warning}
## One hard rule: train on your own series only

The Track B pool cuts several series from the same source, disguised. **Another student's history can
contain your hidden horizon.** A network trained across the other series would be trained on your answer.
Not allowed, and not needed: the foundation models bring the "many series" experience with them.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What the pool says

Measured on all 140 issued series, each forecast made from the full served history and scored on the
hidden horizon. ETS and ARIMA are the automatic ones; the networks use the template's settings.

| Forecast | Beats the benchmark | Within 10% | Worse | Median skill | Worst skill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `AutoETS` + `AutoARIMA` + Chronos-2 | **99%** | 1% | 0% | **0.785** | 1.08 |
| `AutoETS` + `AutoARIMA` + `MSTL` | 96% | 3% | 1% | 0.798 | 1.18 |
| `AutoETS` + `AutoARIMA` | 100% | — | — | 0.805 | 0.93 |
| select the best of `AutoETS`, `AutoARIMA`, `MSTL` on four windows | 96% | 2% | 2% | 0.811 | 1.23 |
| `MSTL` alone | 80% | 6% | 14% | 0.812 | 2.46 |
| Chronos-2 | 84% | 9% | 7% | 0.819 | 2.05 |
| TimesFM 2.5 | 76% | 10% | 14% | 0.837 | 1.61 |
| TiRex | 77% | 11% | 11% | 0.869 | 2.37 |
| N-BEATS, trained on the one series | 57% | 12% | 31% | 0.939 | 3.02 |
| MLP, trained on the one series | 50% | 14% | 36% | 0.997 | 3.48 |
| LSTM, trained on the one series | 46% | 9% | 45% | 1.041 | 4.14 |

- **The pool was screened so that `AutoETS` and `AutoARIMA` each beat the benchmark** — so every row with
  them is flattered by construction. MSTL, the networks and the foundation models were not screened: their
  rows are what you would expect on fresh data.
- **A network trained on one series is close to a coin flip** against the benchmark: a few hundred
  observations are little to learn from.
- **A foundation model alone** beats the benchmark on 76–84% of the series and can lose badly on the
  rest. **Added to the old models** it gave the best median of all — the Week 9 lesson again.
- **Intervals of `AutoETS` + `AutoARIMA` + `MSTL`, on the hidden horizon:** the averaged bounds cover 78%
  of the points on average, the conformal recipe 79%; Winkler scores 3.75 and 3.85. Neither recipe wins
  in general — which is why you choose on your own windows.
- Your Lab 5 and Lab 7 models may not be the automatic ones. The table is a guide, not a promise.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Track C: what the model cards say they were trained on

You do not know your series' source, but you know the families: Track B is cut from public Australian and
US economic statistics.

| Model | Published training data |
|---|---|
| Chronos-2 | Technical report, Table 6: 22 real datasets (M4 monthly, electricity and others) plus synthetic data |
| TimesFM 2.5 | Model card: GIFT-Eval pretraining set (GIFT-Eval paper, Table 14: Monash datasets incl. M1, M3, tourism, Australian electricity, …), Wikimedia pageviews, Google Trends, synthetic data |
| TiRex | Paper, Tables 5–6: subsets of the Chronos and GIFT-Eval training sets |

None of them lists Australian retail turnover or US employment statistics. "Not listed" is not "not
seen": a corpus can contain a series under another name. Say what you can and cannot rule out.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where this goes wrong

- **Choosing on the validation window alone.** Four windows, and the scoreboard's mean — not window 1.
- **Choosing the members or the mix after reading the table.** Then it is a selection in disguise. Write
  the notes in 2.0 and 2.1 first.
- **Reading one seed as the network's score.** A small network on one short series can move a lot from
  seed to seed. Run your best one twice.
- **"New" read as "better".** On many Track B series ETS or ARIMA is still the one to beat.
- **Judging an interval on the windows it was built from.** `interval_check` leaves each window out.
- **Forecasting from `train`.** `final_forecast` calls every forecaster again on the whole of `y`.
- **An API key in the notebook.** TimeGPT is welcome in track D; the key comes from a Colab secret.

📖 [FPP3 §13.4 Forecast combinations](https://otexts.com/fpp3/combinations.html) ·
[§12.4 Neural network models](https://otexts.com/fpp3/nnetar.html) ·
[§5.5 Prediction intervals](https://otexts.com/fpp3/prediction-intervals.html) ·
[Chronos-2 technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15821) ·
[TimesFM 2.5 model card](https://huggingface.co/google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch) ·
[TiRex paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23719)
:::

## 🧹 Section 4 — Code quality and reproducibility (1 point)

- The notebook runs top to bottom on a fresh kernel without errors.
- The submission file is written **by the notebook**, not edited by hand.
- No leakage: everything is compared on the rolling windows; only the final forecast sees all of `y`; no
  network is trained on any series but yours.
- Every number in your text comes from a cell.

## ⏱ How long this should take

About two hours for one track. Section 1 refits three models on four windows — a few minutes for a
monthly ARIMA. Track B trains 12 networks — a few minutes on a CPU; track C needs seconds once the weights
are downloaded. Most of the time should go into Section 3.
